articles.title: My wife and I are in our late 70s and don’t have any children. Who can help us in our old age? | Annalisa Barbieri
articles.summary: Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around. You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involved. My wife and I are in our late 70s, and have been married for more than 40 years. We didn’t have kids and were rather traumatised after failed IVF.
body: My wife is Asian and has no UK-based family. I do, but they are not close geographically, nor are they people who would be able to give any support if needed. Friends are of a similar age and so have their own issues to deal with. My wife and I have always been a self-reliant unit, and we’re both reasonably healthy, but I’m increasingly aware that there will soon come a time when help is needed.

We should make arrangements for things such as a lasting power of attorney (LPA), but there is nobody we would trust enough and who would be willing to take on that role. As social care for older people slips further into crisis, how can we plan for the inevitable? This must be a problem faced by a significant number of people, but it doesn’t seem to be aired.
I think you’re right: this is a growing problem, and I’d be interested to hear what others have done, since, sadly, I cannot magic up someone for you.

I took your issue to two people: psychoanalytic psychotherapist and CEO of Tavistock Relationships Andrew Balfour, author of Life and Death: Our Relationship With Ageing, Dementia and Other Fates of Time; and estate planning specialist solicitor Gary Rycroft to look at the legal side.
points: Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around.
You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involved.
My wife and I are in our late 70s, and have been married for more than 40 years.
My wife and I have always been a self-reliant unit, and we’re both reasonably healthy, but I’m increasingly aware that there will soon come a time when help is needed.

articles.title: It’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiers
articles.summary: From husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in Europe. At Ruka, the first skiers of the year slalomed down the slopes on 2 October.
body: The Narnia-like setting offers just as much action off the runs as on them, and in December the resort launches Ruka Guides, guided adventures from a dedicated activity centre. Spend the morning e-fatbiking through snowy forests (from €90) or cutting a hole in a frozen lake to catch fish (from €89), before learning Arctic survival skills (from €85) or snowshoeing in the evening darkness on the hunt for the northern lights (from €89).

Other, more offbeat diversions include floating in a thermal suit down the freezing Kiveskoski river in meditative silence (from €135), whizzing down an alpine coaster at up to 25mph (from €11.88) and practising your sun salutation in the forest surrounded by grazing reindeer (from €45).

In the depths of winter, the sun sets just a shade after 3.30pm in the Cairngorms national park and doesn’t rise again until about 8.50 the following morning. Those long hours of darkness combined with low levels of light pollution (the area around Tomintoul and Glenlivet is an International Dark Sky Park) makes it the perfect place for stargazing.

articles.title: ‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?
articles.summary: There has been a steep rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years. Is that down to greater understanding – or overdiagnosis? The home of 85-year-old Uta Frith does not exactly look like the latest front in the culture wars.
body: “Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells me. “And then we have a subgroup of people who used to be called neurotic, who have all sorts of mental issues, including anxiety. And a kind of hypersensitivity.”

I have a 20-year-old autistic son, James, who also has learning disabilities – as well as an amazing talent for music – and now goes to a specialist further education college. When he was diagnosed 17 years ago, understanding and awareness of autism seemed to be moving in roughly the right direction. I could never have anticipated the way it has ballooned into a subject of such controversy, which puts me and millions of others in a worldwide community of people who now follow the news with a mixture of bafflement and dread.

articles.title: How to improve your memory: 10 easy, enjoyable expert tips – from reading a book to getting more sleep
articles.summary: Relying on technology can make us forgetful, but there are some simple ways to sharpen your recall. Memory experts describe the tricks and habits that can help. Memory can worsen as we age, but it is often possible to do something about it.
body: Another way that tech can disrupt memory is through its impact on our ability to focus. “We are rapidly switching our attention from one thing to the next,” says Sahakian. “This makes it difficult for people to then focus their attention and concentrate when they need to accomplish a goal. Experiments have shown that students who have mobile phones in class do not perform as well in tests; even having a mobile phone that was off next to you acts as a distractor of your attention.”

Kermode is pretty good at recalling dates. “I’ve got techniques for remembering them, where each month has a particular meaning and/or a colour, and then each day of the month has an object,” she says. “But remembering to actually do something on that birthday – that’s a different thing that I struggle with. I would say that is a different part of the brain.”
points: Relying on technology can make us forgetful, but there are some simple ways to sharpen your recall.
Memory experts describe the tricks and habits that can help.
Memory can worsen as we age, but it is often possible to do something about it.

articles.title: Let’s Give a Big Hand for Heidi Klum’s 2026 Halloween Costume
articles.summary: This year, the queen of Halloween transformed herself into a giant replica of her own hand. “I thought it would be funny and bizarre to take something so familiar and twist it.”
body: The star began ideating on the concept about a year ago—even before her 2025 Halloween bash, when she dressed up as Medusa. “Sometimes an idea comes to me very early, and other times I'm still figuring things out closer to Halloween,” says Klum. “I remember trying to explain it to my costume designer, Mike Marino, and he basically told me that he needed to focus on Medusa first! But it stayed in the back of my mind, and I knew I wanted to bring it to life this year.”

As usual, Klum worked her go-to team of special effects artists to bring her delightfully-kooky vision to life. Mike Marino, her right-hand man, led the work with his ProRenFX team. They began by taking a look at Klum’s very own hand for design inspiration. “[Mike] has all of these scans of my body, so he was able to use those to create an exact replica of my hand,” says Klum. “We wanted everything to be as realistic as possible—the anatomy, the veins, the muscles, all the little details that make a hand look like a real hand.”

articles.title: 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November
articles.summary: Like creamy fondue beans, stuffing-crusted fish, and more cozy meals for chilly nights.
body: As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

The good news? You don’t need to spend your whole Sunday cooking to make dinner feel special, so you’ll have plenty of time for that When Harry Met Sally rewatch. These 21 easy weeknight dinners deliver all the comfort without the commitment. There’s a three-ingredient pumpkin soup, gochujang chicken that gets a quick blast under the broiler, and a smoky one-pan pasta made with pantry staples. Plus a few Thanksgiving -adjacent flavors—sage, stuffing, squash—because the holiday is right around the corner.
points: Like creamy fondue beans, stuffing-crusted fish, and more cozy meals for chilly nights.

articles.title: 13 Books That Changed Comedian, Author, and Drag King Murray Hill’s Life
articles.summary: Hill’s new memoir, “Showbiz!: My Life as a Middle-Aged Man,” is out now from Gallery Books.
body: Hollywood is a strange and mysterious place, even for those who have operated within its orbit for decades. But author, comedian, and drag king Murray Hill’s new memoir, Showbiz!: My Life as a Middle-Aged Man (Gallery Books), sheds an alternately moving and hilarious light on “the industry,” charting Hill’s rise from a fraught New England childhood to a career starring in New York and Boston cabaret shows and appearing on television series including Somebody, Somewhere, Life & Beth, and Elsbeth.
In the latest edition of Vogue ’s Required Reading series, Hill shares a selection of books that have inspired his own memoir and seen him through the ups and downs of Hollywood life.

Kathleen Hanna is a punk-rock icon, feminist trailblazer, and one of my dearest friends. She’s spent her life making noise, breaking rules, and telling the establishment to beat it. What I love about this book is how she writes about the messy, painful, and hilarious realities behind being a revolutionary. She built her own stage, grabbed the microphone, and started a movement. She is my forever inspiration.

articles.title: Gigi Hadid Cut the Ribbon on Her Fourth Guest in Residence Store with Cashmere, Caviar, and Caricatures
articles.summary: Model and founder Gigi Hadid, clad in a shrunken top and tartan skirt, celebrated the debut of her label’s fourth U.S. store—and its very first uptown address.
body: The first surprise was a trio of pretzels twisted into the letters G, I, and R at the entrance. Inside, florists busied themselves preparing custom arrangements, a three-piece band played beneath a sloped skylight, and a caricature artist stationed near the bar had guests voguing for their portraits and later comparing their likenesses.

Martini glasses were filled with one of two things: martinis, of course, but also cigarettes. Meanwhile, caviar in every conceivable configuration made the rounds: atop passed blinis, with potato chips and crème fraîche at a help-yourself station, and even crowning freshly baked potatoes.
